Furthermore, the subsequent section on the indeterminate nature of upholding and violating precepts integrates the preceding two gates.
In the preceding two gates, if one upholds [the precepts], one fully upholds the ten precepts; if one violates them, one fully violates the ten precepts. Therefore, it is said:
Regarding the definitive classification: among the ten,
the first four belong to the category of precepts (śīla), while the latter six belong to the category of vehicles (yāna).
The fourfold classification of the interaction between the vehicle and the precepts is as follows:
if both factors belong to the same category, they fall under the first two gates;
if the two are interwoven, they belong to the meaning intended here.
Therefore, it is said to be indeterminate.
Thus, while these four phrases constitute four texts, they represent two meanings; the intent lies in maintaining both.
Because [the former] is not manifest as the latter, this is explained again.
Regarding the two aspects of "words" and "meaning," these refer to the vehicle (yāna) and the precepts (śīla).
To provide a general discussion below, I shall clarify the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi);
first, I will distinguish between the general and the specific.
If it is said that the ten factors are collectively termed "precepts" (*śīla*) as previously explained—
because the path, concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth are also called precepts—
it may also be said that the ten factors are collectively termed "vehicles" (*yāna*), for all are capable of moving one toward transcendence.
This means that because the first four precepts deliver one from the three miserable realms,
they should be distinguished into four categories according to their specific meanings; thus,
the first four constitute the "precepts" (śīla) and the latter six constitute the "vehicle" (yāna).
Each is further divided into three grades to correspond with the degrees of urgency.
Furthermore, one may also correlate precepts and merit to form four permutations:
having merit but lacking precepts is like a royal elephant.
To have precepts but no merit is like a bhikṣu who begs for food but receives nothing.
To be endowed with both precepts and merit is like a bhikṣu who receives offerings.
To have neither merit nor precepts is like a hungry dog or a hungry ghost.
Furthermore, one should apply the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) regarding the presence or absence of merit and wisdom.
These permutations should fully embody the two adornments of merit and wisdom, with both the vehicle and the precepts held with equal urgency,
such that there is no flaw in either the phenomena or the principle.
The "phenomenal" (shi) corresponds to the former four [stages], while the "principle" (li) corresponds to the latter six.
Since a person of the Perfect Teaching has the capacity to transcend and ascend to the ten stages within a single lifetime,
it is said that these may be attained in one life.
Nanyue said:
"Throughout one's life, one should hope to enter the Bronze Wheel [Vehicle] by merely purifying the six sense faculties.
He further said:
If one can cultivate the four practices of peaceful dwelling, one will attain entry into the six sense organs within a single lifetime;
at the very slowest, it will not exceed three lifetimes.
However, if one acts for the sake of fame and profit, one shall not attain it for many kalpas.
Those of dull and sharp faculties in the *Avataṃsaka* are simply those of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings];
the number of their grades can be seen by measuring them according to the previous exposition.
The second phrase means that they are not equally urgent.
As stated in the Mahāyāna sūtras, one might suddenly hear the Dharma while in the body of a being in the evil realms,
yet one will never fail to hear the Dharma when in the bodies of humans or devas.
Upon hearing the Dharma, there will be a limit to birth and death.
Humans and devas may otherwise regress and enter the three evil realms;
since the text speaks from the perspective of those with the most severe [afflictions], it says that "all are devoured."

Although all five categories of offenses have been violated and both body and speech are entirely deficient, the seeds planted in past lives still remain, enabling one to specialize in the principles of the precepts.
Because their faculties are sharp, they may yet attain the Way; therefore, it is better to be strict regarding the vehicle while being lenient regarding the precepts.
Regarding the mention of "Zhendan" (China) in the third sentence:
this refers to the period when the Buddha was still in the world;
had the teachings flowed to this land [during his lifetime], one would have known [of them] but not seen [him].
The two characters "Zhēndān" (振丹) are both likely scribal errors;
the tenth citation below uses "Zhèndàn" (震旦).
Master Lín explains: [text follows].
The East belongs to the Trigram Zhen, the direction from which the sun rises;
hence it is called Zhendan (China).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* calls it Zhina.
The *Xiyu ji* states that "Zhìnà" (Cīna) is a sound closely resembling "Zhèndàn" (Zhendan) and "Zhēndān" (Zhendan); therefore,
it is known that all these belong to the Sanskrit phonetic system.
Regarding "three hundred million households" and so forth,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 11, states:
"In Śrāvastī, there were nine hundred million households."
Three hundred million saw the Buddha with their eyes;
three hundred million heard him with their ears but did not see him;
three hundred million neither heard nor saw him.
The Buddha resided in Śrāvastī for twenty-five years, yet these people neither heard nor saw him;
how much less so the devas who are attached to pleasure?
This also applies to those born in places where it is difficult to encounter the Dharma.
The northern continent, the three evil realms, the long-lived heavens, those before and after the Buddhas, and those with impaired faculties—
these constitute the eight difficulties.
To explain this and resolve lingering doubts, the following analogy is provided.
A doubt arises:
"Since one does not encounter a Buddha, what need is there for these precepts?
Therefore, it is explained through an analogy: "One hopes to encounter a general amnesty."
To receive amnesty is to encounter a Buddha and hear the Dharma.
In the past, one did not cultivate the vehicle and lacked the conditions for hearing the Dharma;
thus, remaining within the three realms is like being imprisoned.
Precepts and virtues are like wealth;
the paths of action are like great power;
obtaining the bodies of humans and devas is like life not yet having ended.
Or, encountering the Buddha-dharma as one encounters a general amnesty,
yet fearing that beings in the realms of humans and devas might still not be transformed,
he therefore further rebukes them, saying:
If one does not cultivate the vehicle, one will never encounter a Buddha;
when the merits of humans and devas are exhausted, one falls back into the three miserable realms.
Therefore, know that the cultivation of the vehicle must by no means be omitted.
Below, in the "Examination of Practitioners," it says: "This refers to those who come by way of provisional means to lead others to the ultimate reality.
Since their precepts are lax while their pursuit of the vehicle is urgent, they fall into the three miserable realms.
He will certainly lead them by means of fellow Dharma-body Bodhisattvas;
he will even plant seeds and entice those whose vehicle and precepts are both lax.
Thus, he subtly imparts the teachings to distinguish cause and effect.
Regarding the discernment of causes through the four teachings: the different contemplative wisdoms cultivated in the past according to the four teachings serve as the seeds for the vehicles.
Now, the different attainments of the Way throughout the five flavors clarify their respective fruits.
In the fourth section, on the purification through repentance (*sānti*),
first there is an inquiry:
"Since one has committed transgressions, what is the method for repenting according to both principle and phenomena?"
If one commits an offense of the lower category,
one first answers by repenting for the light offenses.
According to the Vinaya texts, from the second category downward, all contain methods for repentance.
Only when confession has brought about the purity of the precepts do śamatha and vipaśyanā become clear.
How could one possibly hold the precepts lightly while still pursuing the principles?
If one commits a grave offense among the transgressions, [the precepts are lost].
This means that when attachment results in a grave offense,
it cannot be extinguished merely by changing one's perspective; rather,
one must rely on samādhi, entrusting oneself to phenomena while adhering to principle, and employing the contemplation of signs as an antidote.
Only then can one be purified.
Below, the ten states of mind in both reverse and direct order are clarified;
these constitute the method for repentance.
Therefore, it is said that this further clarifies [the previous point].
Next, the section on "Contemplation of Principle" below clarifies how, due to biased views and understanding,
one has not yet reached the point where body and speech refrain from committing light or grave offenses.
Furthermore, there is no need to employ the four kinds of samādhi;
it is sufficient simply to turn the contemplation so that the mind of right view naturally vanishes.

Since one's deviance has not yet been manifested to others, one merely bows the head and reproaches oneself. If one’s views are heavy, one should return to the contemplative mind to practice repentance.
Since it is said that for those who have committed grave offenses, one does not rely on contemplation of the mind alone,
"contemplation of the mind" means that when performing ritual repentance, one must necessarily rely upon the contemplation of the mind.
If there is no contemplative mind, grave offenses will not be extinguished;
because contemplation is primary, it says "within the contemplative mind.
This cites the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* as the sublime and supreme meditative concentration.
One must act in accordance with principle before one can accomplish the aforementioned matters.
Regarding the phrase "the Vaipulya scriptures and so forth":

if one violates the Three Refuges by taking refuge in false teachers, false teachings, or false assemblies, thereby breaking the five precepts or even the grave offenses among the two hundred and fifty precepts.
Thus, one becomes a Buddha while still in the state of death;
because the precepts are restored through repentance, it is said that one is "reborn.
Nanshan also established the method of Repentance for Non-arising (*amutpāda-saṃvara*), enumerating three types in total.
First, the fact that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of self—
when this principle illuminates the mind, it is called the Hīnayāna.
Second, that the fundamental characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
It is merely the deluded vision of sentient beings.
This principle of illumination and function belongs to the small-bodhisattvas.
Third, external objects among all phenomena are fundamentally without reality.
This principle is profound and subtle, to be known only through mental perception;
it is the practice for realizing the fruit of Buddhahood by the great Bodhisattvas.
Although this passage from Nanshan provides a scriptural basis, [it remains so].
However, the first judgment belongs to the Hīnayāna;
in the Hīnayāna, there is already no principle for repenting grave offenses,
let alone in this stage which is already separated from the initial mind.
The second and third [stages] further belong to the Bodhisattvas and the fruit of Buddhahood;
for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is no ground upon which they can rely or fix their minds.
What is established here directly clarifies the state of the lowliest of ordinary beings.
Those who wish to employ the Mahāyāna to repent of grave offenses should rely on such texts as the Vaipulya *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*. For this reason,
Nanshan judged that the stage [of these practices] is too high for those at the initial stage of the path to have any part in them.
Since those in high positions are without fault, why list them?
If one clarifies the duration of others' inferiority, it does not extend beyond the past and present.
Yet, when one contemplates the ten mental states, they are traced back to the beginningless ignorance and perversion.
What sin would not be extinguished?
Furthermore, there are fools in the world who claim that because the mind is unborn, all phenomena are likewise non-existent, and thus they commit no new sins.
Now, those who create transgressions necessarily rely upon the three poisons.
For one who has truly realized non-arising, even merit is not produced, let alone transgression;
this is because both transgression and merit alike accord with the cycle of birth and death.
Regarding "repentance":
as stated in the seventeenth fascicle of the Mahāyāna Sūtra, Jīvaka said to King Ajātaśatru,
"Cultivating a single virtuous thought can destroy a million kinds of evil."
Just as a small amount of vajra can destroy Mount Sumeru,
just as a small fire can burn everything,
and just as a small amount of poison can harm sentient beings.
It is the same with minor virtues: they can destroy great evils.
Although they are called "minor virtues," in reality they are great.
For this reason, one must perform repentance.
Repentance is simply the cultivation of goodness through the three karmas.
Within this text, twenty meanings are established and divided into three pairs;
the underlying intent varies according to its range, whether far-reaching or immediate.
Regarding the statement "three pairs":
first, the inverse and the conforming; second, craving and views; third, phenomena and principle.
The inverse and the conforming constitute the functional capacity.
Attachment and views are the causes of transgression;
phenomena and principle are what is revealed.
Regarding "near" and "far": "near" refers to immediate purification, while "far" refers to the aspiration for correct practice.
Within this, first are listed the ten minds that follow the current, arranged from subtle to coarse.
The first arises from a single thought of beginningless ignorance,
culminating in the accomplishment of the sins of an icchantika.
Next, the ten minds of the counter-flow proceed from the coarse to the subtle;
therefore, one first overturns and destroys the offenses of the icchantika, and only then reaches the emptiness of the nature of ignorance.
Previously, within the flow-with-the-stream, view and craving likewise proceeded from the subtle to the coarse, following along with birth and death.
Therefore, they are collectively established under one gate in accordance with the flow [of samsara].
It is only upon reaching the counter-flow that love and views are differentiated.
Regarding the mention of "arrogance" and so forth within the initial stage of the flow:
"Shamelessness" refers to an appearance of non-compliance.
Next is the concluding summary of the preceding section and the clarification of the purpose for what follows.
Next, "flowing against the current" has two parts.
First there is affection, followed by vision.
Regarding the initial affection:
it occurs at the outset of correctly believing in cause and effect.
The "feeble one" refers to the manifest [self].
"Alas, you who have no hook!"—this is an exclamation of startled alarm.
It means: "I know that in my past lives I was a person devoid of shame."
Now I am filled with self-reproach,
for in the past I lacked the hook of faith, which led me to commit grave offenses;
like a mad elephant without a hook, I was impossible to restrain.
Now, one uses the hook of shame (*hrī*) to hook the elephant of the shameless mind (*āhrīkya*).
Therefore, the Great Sūtra states that there are two pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) capable of saving sentient beings:
first, shame; second, dread of blame (*ottappa*).
Shame (*hrī*) is not committing an offense oneself;
remorse (*apatrāpya*) is disclosing it to others.
Furthermore, shame is internal self-reproach.
"Vrīḍā" (shame) means not causing others to act [unrighteously];
"apatrāpya" (modesty) refers to feeling shame before heaven and so forth—these various interpretations differ.
If one lacks both shame and modesty, they are called an animal.
"To last for a thousand years" is merely a conventional expression;
once one loses this human body, it will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas.
"Mien-miao" (綿邈) describes the quality of being vast and remote.
On the long journey through the three realms, one should take the myriad practices as provisions;
in the vast ocean of birth and death, one should take wisdom as a boat and raft.
Therefore, one should fear impermanence and prepare provisions and cultivate a boat and raft in advance.
Once one closes one's eyes [in death], whom else can one rely upon?
Therefore, it is said, "Where can one find security?
This law of impermanence is something abandoned by the noble ones (ārya), for it is not to be relied upon.
Having no mother to rely upon and no father to depend on,
being unable to bring forth the supramundane body of virtue,
they are called "those without reliance."
Regarding the phrase "when one's years have somewhat passed," this refers to the passing of years as a point of discourse.
As for the "wind-knife" (vāyu-śastra),
when a person's life is about to end, they are inevitably disintegrated by the dispersing winds produced by the power of karma.
It is like dismantling a bellows so that the wind of breath no longer continues;
it is like breaking up a drainage ditch so that the blood vessels no longer flow;
it is like disassembling a mechanical device so that the tendons and joints no longer respond.
It is like extinguishing the warmth of a torch by breaking it;
it is like the separation of flesh and bone when a clay vessel is shattered.
Once the four elements have been divided, one must surely encounter suffering and ruin.
How can one remain with hands folded in idleness without cultivating the roots of goodness?
Regarding the jackal,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, states:
For example, it is like a jackal dwelling among the trees in a forest,
relying upon lions, tigers, leopards, and the like,
seeking their leftover meat to sustain its own life.
During the empty interval of time at midnight, he leaped over the city walls.
He entered deeply into private dwellings seeking meat but found none;
fleeing to avoid pursuit, he fell asleep and did not wake until the end of the night, remaining terrified and without recourse throughout.
When he first intended to set out on his journey, he feared he would not escape;
while staying there, fearing the agony of death, he feigned death and lay upon the ground.
When the crowd came and saw him, they [believed him dead].
One person said, "I need a jackal's ears," and he immediately cut them off.
The jackal thought to himself:
"Though cutting off my ears is painful, it will at least leave my body intact.
Then another person came and said he required its tail.
He thought to himself again, "Cutting off the tail is a minor matter."
Next, another person said, "I need a jackal’s tooth.
The jackal thought to itself,
"Those who come to take me are becoming more numerous."
"If he were to take my head, there would be no way for me to survive.
He immediately rose from the ground and, exerting all his strength with supreme valor,
braved the perils and traversed the terrain until he finally managed to save himself.
The mind of the practitioner seeking liberation from suffering and hardship is likewise thus:
to fail to practice when young is like losing one's ears;
to fail to practice when old is like losing one's tail.
If one does not practice while ill— like having lost a tooth—
how could one possibly wait until death, which would be like losing one's head?
That one remains complacent even during old age and illness [shows a lack of urgency].
There may be a slight delay.
As for the matter of death, I shall not be extravagant, knowing that there is no hope [of survival].
As for those such as King Aśoka and others...
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 20, states:
"In King Aśoka’s palace, sixty thousand arhats were constantly provided with offerings.
King Aśvaghoṣa was the younger brother of King Aśoka."
Every time he saw the assembly of monks receiving offerings from the king,
he would ask, "How can they receive offerings constantly?
The king replied:
"Although he has received [the throne], he constantly contemplates impermanence; what leisure does he have for greedy attachment?
His younger brother was constantly skeptical and did not believe this.
The King, wishing to subdue him, secretly dispatched a man to instruct him to usurp the royal throne.
The king then waited for him and asked,
"Do you have two lords in your country?
He was about to execute him when—
Furthermore, let him rule over Jambudvīpa for seven days;
after this period, he shall be put to death.
Within these seven days, let him indulge his desires at will through the five objects of sensory pleasure.
When one day had passed, he immediately ordered a caṇḍāla to ring a bell and announce:
"One day has already passed; six days remain before death."
When the seven days had thus passed, he shook his bell and said, "The seven days have elapsed; today you shall die.
The king then asked:
"Does the Lord of Jambudvīpa enjoy himself with full delight?
He replied,
"I have neither seen, nor heard, nor perceived it at all."
Why is this? For the caṇḍāla daily rings his bell and proclaims in a loud voice:
"Of the seven days, this many days have already passed."
"In so many days I shall die.
Although I am the lord of Jambudvīpa and possess exquisite fivefold sensual pleasures,
because my grief is so profound, I neither hear nor see them.
Therefore, one should know that the power of much pleasure is weak.
If a person experiences pleasure throughout their entire body while being pricked by a needle in a single spot,
all the pleasure ceases entirely and they perceive only the piercing pain.
The King said,
"Monks are likewise;
they merely contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self."
What leisure is there to greedily crave offerings and sustenance?
On the contrary, one who breaks [this resolve] does not fear the evil realms;
such a person should contemplate those evil realms as if hearing the sound of a bell—their heads shall soon be severed.
The *Dharmapada* states:
Formerly, there was a lord of devas who knew for himself that his life had ended and he would be reborn among donkeys.
Distressed beyond measure, he said:
"The one who can save us from suffering and calamity is only the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, they went to the Buddha's dwelling, prostrated themselves on the ground, and took refuge in the Buddha.
Before they had even risen, their lives came to an end, and they were reborn in the womb of a donkey.
The bit snapped, severing the potter’s clay vessel;
the potter struck it, and it subsequently injured the fetus, which then re-entered the body of the Heavenly Emperor.
The Buddha said:
"At the moment of death, he took refuge in the Triple Gem, and having thus completed his karmic retribution for his offenses,
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, heard this and attained the first fruit [of the path].
Therefore, even a temporary taking of refuge can overturn and destroy the mind directed toward the evil realms."
Regarding "confession," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Dà jīng), fascicle 17, states:
"The wise person is of two kinds.
The first is one who, by nature, does not commit evil."
Second, confessing one's faults to others.
There are likewise two types of fools:
first, those who commit transgressions.
Second is concealment.
The external defects of jade are called flaws (*xia*);
the internal defects of jade are called blemishes (*ci*).
Therefore, this can serve as an analogy for the two faults of concealment and manifestation.
To cover up one's flaws is called a lack of shame and remorse (*ahrīkya-ānapatrāpya*).
As for "thieves, poison, and noxious weeds," and so forth:
If one confesses,
it is like searching for a thief so they cannot remain hidden;
it is like pruning a poisonous tree, for if left uncut, its evil will grow.
It is like pulling out weeds; if left behind, they will spread and entangle.
Regarding the phrase "the roots are exposed":
for all transgressions arise from the concealment of the mind.
If one overturns the previously concealed mind— like cutting down a tree at its root or exhausting a stream at its source—
then the branches will wither and the flow will cease. However, if the concealment remains as it was,
the offense is a cause of evil and, being concealed, shall not be extinguished.
Because people conceal their transgressions, they become unwholesome persons.
"Wholesome" (ryō) means good.
Regarding "Kāśyapa and others":
The Buddha valued the extinguishing of offenses according to the individual's capacity;
whether committed privately or among a group, there was no fixed rule.
As the Seventeenth Fascicle of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra states:
To conceal [one's faults] is outflow;
not to conceal them is called being without outflows.
If one commits a transgression and does not conceal it, then that transgression becomes slight.
Regarding "other practices and dharmas" and so forth:
this refers to all other sutras besides the Vaipulya and Dhūta [teachings],
such as the *Pratyutpanna*, the *Sīhanāda*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and others, as well as the monastic regulations for the six periods of daily practice.
It does not say that those who approach others are of the same class.
As for the phrase "like a hidden abscess," it means that when one commits a transgression without it being revealed, it is like a hidden abscess beneath the skin.
"If, upon receiving a subsequent report, it is as previously stated, then one is dead;

if it is indeed as determined, etc., then after performing a single confession, one gives rise to a decisive realization and attains the state of being free from transgression—this is called 'fruition' (phala)."
It is resolute. Therefore, one must sever the offering so that it does not continue further.
As for those who have committed an offense for the first time and so forth:
This was an original pardon.
Having already received a pardon at the outset, a second offense is difficult to condone;
thus one knows that when a crime is repeated, it is difficult to extinguish.
Therefore, one must sever the continuity of the mind.
Thus, the analogy of vomiting is used for confession: to commit the offense again after having confessed is like eating once more.
As the treatise says:
Having already renounced the pleasures of the five desires and cast them aside without looking back,
how could one wish to obtain them again, like a fool who eats his own vomit?
This is the case for those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta.
If one were to simply extinguish transgressions in this manner, why would it be necessary to arouse the bodhicitta?
For instance, in the Hīnayāna, there are two types of repentance— communal and individual—
which fail to overturn the objects of transgression from beginningless time in their entirety.
The provisional texts of the Lesser Vehicle regarding the extinction of transgressions all stem from the failure to resolve upon bodhicitta;
furthermore, the repentances of the Hīnayāna are merely termed "reproving."
There is no principle of non-requital for the sake of protecting others;
it is in order to reverse such [views] that one generates the bodhicitta.
The rest is as explained in the text.
Regarding those who cultivate merit to compensate for transgressions:
the offenses committed since beginningless time necessarily pervade the three karmas.
Because they are pervasive, they continue; because they continue, they become heavy.
Therefore, one must now cultivate merit to compensate for past transgressions;
the three karmas must operate in unison,
with mindfulness and exertion continuing uninterruptedly from moment to moment without ceasing.
Regarding "not by shifting [the burden]" and so forth:
past offenses are as deep and vast as the ocean, while the three karmas operating together are like a mountain.
How could the mountain of the three operating karmas ever fill the ocean of the three transgressions?
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the Śrīmālā-sūtra," it means that causing the present dharma not to perish is called "guarding the true dharma."
To gather the medicinal teachings without weariness is called embracing the true Dharma.
Regarding "associating with evil friends" and so forth:
it is because evil associates can destroy a person's roots of goodness for enlightenment.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle 20, states:
"Just as wicked elephants and the like can only destroy an impure and foul body,
so too is the evil spiritual friend."
It can destroy the pure body.
Whether it be the physical body or the Dharma-body, whether it reaches the three realms of existence or does not reach the three realms of existence,
the same applies to bodily enemies and Dharma-enemies.
Regarding the phrase "mindfulness of unimpeded loving-kindness" and so forth:
loving-kindness is able to accord with sentient beings as one's own virtuous friend,
thereby reversing one's former intimacy with evil persons.
Wisdom can shatter heterodoxy and guide me from delusion and deviation;
it overturns my former reliance on the words of evil friends and brings full realization of greed, hatred, and ignorance.
Regarding "seeking until the self cannot be found":
formerly, from the state of non-abiding, one gave rise to the view of a self and even to greed and hatred;
now, however, one traces back greed and hatred to their point of origin in non-abiding.
When the root is destroyed, the branches naturally fall;
that which is conceived here is not the true self (ātman),
but is merely a provisional name based on beginningless false conceptualization.
Regarding the "gate of tranquility":
because one attains tranquility through the contemplation of the mind,
all states of mind constitute the gate of tranquility.
The Sūtra further states:
"Because it demonstrates tranquility.
Since one is able to perceive tranquility by means of the various minds, [it is so called].
Just as one sees a destination by means of a guide,
the first fascicle of the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* states:
"In the eastern land of Adorned, there is a Buddha named Light-Aspect (*Prabhāsa-lakṣaṇa*)."
He is currently preaching the Dharma.
There is a great śrāvaka named Jñānapradīpa who,
when questioned by Mañjuśrī, remained silent and did not answer.
That Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"You may preach a Dharma-gate so that all sentient beings may attain the unsurpassed path.
Mañjuśrī replied:
All phenomena are gates of tranquility,
for they demonstrate tranquility.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmavīra.
He asked Mañjuśrī,
"The Tathāgata has taught that greed, hatred, and delusion are gates to tranquility;
does he thereby demonstrate tranquility?"
Mañjuśrī asked,
"From what do the three poisons arise?
He replied:
Deluded thoughts arise;
deluded thoughts abide in inversion; inversion abides in the notion of "mine";
and the notion of "mine" abides in the view of a self-existent body.
The view of a self-body abides in the view of a self;

yet the view of a self has no place of abiding. Each and every phrase consists of one question and one answer, as fully detailed in the first sentence. Thus, when one searches for this view of a self throughout the ten directions, it is entirely unfindable.
For this reason, I say that all dharmas are gates of tranquility.
Herein, the meaning of that sūtra passage is employed in its entirety; it is merely a concise expression, which can be understood by comparison.
Regarding the statement "if one says 'equal'" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:

Second, listening to the true Dharma;
third, contemplating its meaning;
fourth, practicing according to the teachings.
If it is said that the diligent practice of asceticism is the proximate cause for Great Nirvāṇa,
such a thing is impossible.
Next is the repentance for the sin of [wrong] views.
This refers back to the ten minds that flow with the current mentioned previously;
since those preceding minds that flow with the current listed both craving and views together,
the present repentance for views reiterates the flow with the current once more.
He again points to the preceding list.
Previously, he distinguished the "mind of love" (*anunaya-citta*) from the downward-flowing [impulses];
both the mind of love and the upward-flowing [impulses] are merely attachments to phenomena.

Attachment belonging to the dull defilements is called the "offense of the dull defilements," which does not mean that the offense has been extinguished or that the dull defilements have already been exhausted.
Because that offense of attachment arises dependent upon a specific object,
it is therefore repented by means of that object.
When one perceives a transgression against principle, the arising of repentance must likewise accord with principle.
If one repents of grave offenses, they must also be practiced in conjunction [with ritual action].
Therefore, it is said: "When heavy afflictions arise, one should employ external rites as an aid."
Supplementary medicines are like the principles of reasoning, while auxiliary aids are like the husks of beans;
thus, both the facts and the principles each have their peripheral and primary aspects.
This is followed by a refutation and then a formal explanation.
This also proceeds from the coarse to the subtle.
What is called "lack of faith" is the mind of an icchantika.
The mind of an icchantika arises from the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Therefore, it is pointed out so that one may recognize suffering and its origin.
Why? Because by virtue of the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there are eighty-eight [afflictions].
Because they are accumulated, they are able to bring about suffering,
as explained in detail in the fifth fascicle.
Regarding the example of Udraka and others:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 19, states:
"One who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception possesses the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Day after day, he flies into the royal palace to eat."
The king’s consort, following the laws of her country, prostrated herself at his feet.
Because she touched his feet, her desire was aroused and she lost her supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
She requested a chariot and departed, returning to her original mountain where she again cultivated the five supernormal powers.

With single-minded devotion, he was on the verge of attaining meditative concentration when the forest and pond upon which he relied were disturbed by the clamor of various fish and birds; consequently,
he made a malicious vow to devour all those fish and birds.
Later, returning as before, he attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and was reborn in that realm.
When his retribution was exhausted, he was drawn back by his former vow and fell into the body of a flying cat.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
The flying cat has a body fifty yojanas wide;
its two wings extend fifty yojanas apart each,
and its total body length is five hundred yojanas.
Having made evil vows, they kill sentient beings—whether moving in water, on land, or through the air—with none escaping;

Consequently, they fall into the body of a flying fox.
This is precisely suffering.
When Sūṣita attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,

Therefore, one discusses humans and devas by encompassing all three truths.
Regarding the explanation of karmic retribution and so forth,
the "Chapter on Faith and Slander" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:

For immeasurable billions of kalpas, they shall fall into the hells,
passing from one hell to another.

or, even if they obtain a human body, they will be born blind from birth;
or they will be born into the families of caṇḍālas.
They remove filth and carry corpses to people's homes;
they may be missing an eye, a tongue, an ear, or a hand,
or they may undergo various kinds of suffering among the animal realm.
Śāriputra asked,
"Is this person similar to one who has committed the five heinous crimes?
The Buddha said:
It exceeds the five heinous crimes.
Even if one listens to their words and believes their speech, one will likewise undergo such suffering.
Since it involves sufferings equal to death and the like, there is no need to inquire further.

There are two causes and conditions for which the Buddha did not speak."

whether they believe it or not.

due to this anxiety and terror, their vital winds will be stirred, causing them to vomit hot blood and die.
If one does not believe, they will undergo even more severe suffering.
Regarding the phrase "turning back and destroying those who do not fear the evil realms," this single clause is explained according to the preceding and following context.
The meaning of the critique of the logical perspective (*yukti-vicāra*) should be stated according to precedent:
"In the past, based on [erroneous] views, one gave rise to faults that destroyed correct reasoning."
They do not fear the three miserable realms.
Now, while they rejoice in the principle of the Truths, they still fear the evil paths of the three emptinesses and the three unconditioned states of the Hinayana,
and even fear the evil paths of the three preceding teachings.
How much more so for the three miserable paths, such as the hells;
for now, we shall consider the meaning of falling into these evil destinies from the perspective of slandering the Three Truths.
"By means of the Eightfold Noble Path, etc.
means that it is only through the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) Eightfold Path that one can destroy the three delusions.
"Because there are [delusions] that are boundless, etc. means...
"Existence" refers to tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*).
"Sin" refers to the retribution (*phala*) summoned by such tainted karma.
This extends even to the sins summoned by that which is untainted (*anāsrava*), both tainted and untainted, and neither tainted nor untainted, resulting in rebirth in the two lands.
Therefore, we know that in the past, delusion regarding the three truths involved karma pervading the three afflictions,
and suffering pervaded the three lands;
now, by taking the Dharma-realm as an object, one gives rise to the bodhicitta.
The unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) also arises pervading the entire dharma-realm;
therefore, it is able to overturn and destroy evil throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Regarding the third truth reaching the "Precious Torch":
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the Bodhisattva’s Jewel Torch Dhāraṇī;
they are precisely the truth of the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārgasatya*)."
Being fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma is called a treasure;
universally illuminating the dharma-realm is called a torch;
and upholding all things is called dhāraṇī.
If one cultivates such merit, what fault could not be remedied?
Even if one were to abandon the view of existence and enter into the view of non-existence.
Furthermore, if one does not cultivate the factors of enlightenment, one will not transcend birth and death.
As for the statement "now knowing existence and so forth," it means that even now one knows that which is neither existent nor non-existent.
How much more so regarding existence and non-existence?
To speak of "existence and non-existence" is merely to provide a brief illustration.
Although one may recognize these faults, one has not yet cultivated the foundations of mindfulness and the like.
If one refutes the lower [levels] by practicing the path-factors through analytical dharma (*vibhajya-dharma*),
then since even the substantial view (*tattva-dṛṣṭi*) of the lower [levels] is already refuted by the general and specific [teachings], how much more so the Tripitaka? Therefore,
it is said that the substantial view is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
Regarding the term "equal" (等), the character "longitudinal" (縱) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*).
To proceed from the shallow toward the profound is termed "longitudinal.
All views are thereby shattered, and all factors of the path (*mārga-dharma*) are cultivated.
Therefore, it is said that this supplements the error of vertical views.
Previously, due to views, one created various views within the realm; since these views have no distinction of depth or shallowness, they are called horizontal.
Now that the cultivation of merit is already profound and the shattering of views is likewise far-reaching,
one begins by using external views to shatter the entry into the External (Hīnayāna) Treasury,
and continues until using distinct views to shatter the entry into the Distinct (Pratyekabuddha), culminating in the Perfect [Entry].
Ultimate perfection is called neither moving nor non-moving, neither practicing nor not practicing;
this is the category of the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). If one were to fully elaborate upon it using the fourfold logical formulation (*catuṣkoṭi*):
One should say: "moving cultivation," "non-moving non-cultivation," and "both moving and non-moving, both cultivating and non-cultivating."
It is neither moving nor non-moving, neither practicing nor non-practicing.
Furthermore, by applying four movements to correspond with one practice,
sixteen phrases are formed.
Now, for the time being, the four cultivations are established in opposition to the four movements;
therefore, they are explained separately.
Because one enters them progressively and vertically, they are called "vertical" (*tiryak*).

Since anything that has not yet accorded with the principle of perfection is termed a "defect," one cultivates the practice of the single mind and the three truths to remedy the shortcomings of the preceding sequential realization of the three truths.
Those who protect the True Dharma formerly disparaged principle while defending views in order to expound those views;
now they disparage views while defending principle in order to expound that principle.
If one does not sacrifice their own body to preserve the Dharma,
how can they manifest their resolve to protect it?
If the resolve to protect the Dharma is weak...
How, then, could one instead protect views that destroy the good?
For this reason, it is further likened to parents protecting their children.
This refers to those who mindfully recollect the Buddhas of the ten directions.
In the past, you internally harbored various views and externally relied on evil teachers;
thus, you followed along with the three delusions and turned your back on the principle of the Three Truths.
Now, you internally contemplate the Three Truths.
The Truths are themselves the Buddha.
Because they are fully endowed both internally and externally,
one is able to overturn and destroy intimacy with evil friends.
If that is so, how can the principle of nature (dharmatā) be the Buddha? Therefore,
he cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Sadāprarudita saw the Buddha in the sky;
later, seeing Dharmodgata,
he then asked him:
"From where does the Buddha come?
He replied,
"Neither coming nor going— this is the Buddha."
The dharma of non-arising is itself the Buddha.
Therefore, one should know that the awakening to the wisdom of non-arising is itself the Buddha. If this is so, then...
The Dharma is itself the Buddha;
therefore, one is able to overturn former evil dharmas and evil teachers.
This refers to those who contemplate that the nature of offenses is empty.
Because one initially adheres to the notion of substantial reality, one does not understand that nature is empty.
In every single thought-moment, the three delusions are fully present;
yet these very three delusions are fundamentally and originally nirvana.
Therefore, it is called "quiescence.
Now, by observing what follows, one clarifies the vision of the emptiness of nature:
when one is empty, all are empty.
The following explains the preceding section on the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
It is feared that one might think that because things are like illusions— neither coming nor going—
they are merely empty.
Therefore, it is reiterated that "one emptiness is all emptiness," and so forth.
The phrase "carrying this" below serves as a summary.
One must contemplate the principle and augment it with phenomena for the rite of repentance to be perfected.
Regarding the statement that he is called the second "heroic son," the Great Sūtra says:
"There are two heroic sons."
First, their nature does not commit evil;
second, having committed it, they are able to repent.
If one considers this life, the delusions of view have not yet arisen.
If one discusses that which is beginningless, who does not possess it?
Thus, we know that all things lack the first [of the four conditions].
Question:
Question: Since the view has not yet arisen, why is it necessary to perform repentance?
Answer:
One reaches [the realization] in advance even before it arises.
Moreover, it was previously shown that one must perform this repentance for those [afflictions] that have already arisen and those that are about to arise.
Therefore, the preceding text refers to the evil of craving and views as "already arisen" and "not yet arisen."
Therefore, the present text merely instructs one to employ these ten minds of reversal and compliance to extinguish the evils of the three periods of time.
Thus, those who practice repentance must practice both the phenomenal and the principled together.
This is called the "lower double conclusion," summarizing the preceding two types of repentance: the phenomenal and the principled.
If the method of repentance is perfected, the samādhi of the three truths and all practices will be fully realized;
how much more so when the ten precepts encompass all conduct?
Samādhi is the eye, and the wisdom of the eye is fully perfected.
It is only upon reaching the stage of the first abode that it is termed "development.
Although the text follows a sequential order, this is done to manifest its perfect interfusion;
all preceding and succeeding passages are likewise so.
Moreover, since the precepts of practice serve as the foundation for the three contemplations,
it is said that "śīla must be pure," and so forth.
If one lacks the precepts of practice, even worldly dhyāna will not exist.
How much more so regarding the three truths!
It is erroneous for those who say that since this is the Mahāyāna, there is no need to uphold the precepts;
as for those who say one should not uphold them, they are mistaken.
This is to maintain without grasping; if one were to call it "non-grasping" by means of not maintaining at all,
that would be the destruction of grasping—
how then could it be called non-grasping?
If even grasping does not exist,
where can forgetting and grasping abide?
Having attained this, the conclusion below establishes the dharma encompassed by eye-wisdom.
Furthermore, it can conclude the preceding sections by establishing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Thus, one knows that the concluding summary serves the original intent.
The section on the purity of upholding the precepts summarizes the names listed previously as well as the characteristics of their observance.
This constitutes the remote preparatory practice for correct cultivation.
With sincere and earnest intent, he concludes the preceding discussion on transgressions and their purification through repentance;
or perhaps he fears that there may be both past and present offenses regarding both principle and phenomena.
Furthermore, one should sincerely repent for those grave transgressions;
once the transgressions are eliminated and one is purified again, there will be no blemish in either of the two worlds,
and this may serve as a condition equivalent to having never committed the offense in the first place.
Therefore, it is said that both serve as the primary conditions; this is the intended meaning here.
○ Regarding the second section, "The Abundance of Clothing and Food," first, the reason for introducing it is as follows:
These robes and food serve as direct conditions for the Path.
As for what is called "the Path," there are those who merely cover their bodies and sustain their lives, yet do not practice the Path.
Since the obstruction of the factors of the Path must first affect the physical life,
if the physical life is established, the foundation of the Path will exist; therefore,
it is said that [the former] "reaches" [the latter].
Between these two conditions, clothing is remote while food is proximate;
therefore, it is cited as scriptural proof that "it is through food that one attains the Way."
Regarding the phrase "although these are minor conditions" and so forth:
however, this clothing and food are fundamentally the conditions for the physical body and its retribution-life;
therefore, they are called "minor conditions."
Relying on this, one is further able to accomplish the matters of the Way and the Dharma;
hence it is called the "Great Matter.
Because there is no clothing, one is naked; because there is no food, one is famished.
In this way, how could one exclusively cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
As for the character "焉" (*yān*), if it is used as an auxiliary sound, it should be pronounced with the *yì-lián* (矣連) rhyme;
however, following its current gloss, it should be pronounced with the *wū-lián* (於連) rhyme. Why? As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 20, states:
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva requires robes or other necessities, he takes them immediately.
Although he accepts food and drink, it is not for the sake of his body;
rather, it is always for the sake of the True Dharma and never for the sake of his physical frame.
One does not cause harm to others.
It is like a person who, having recovered from an illness, applies ghee and parched grain flour to the nine orifices where secretions leak,
and covers them with a cloth.
Regarding "clothing," the following provides the formal explanation.
As for "preventing ugliness and the like," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
As for the robes one receives,
they are not for the purpose of adorning the body,
but for the purpose of covering shame and modesty, and warding off cold, heat, mosquitoes, and gadflies.
What is now called "adornment" refers to concealing the ugliness of one's body and calling it adornment;
it does not mean polishing and adorning oneself in accordance with one's own greedy passions.
Regarding the three types of robes,
they are divided into three grades. Furthermore,
there are the cases of the heavenly Subhūti, the Bhikṣu Mānava, and those permitted to possess heavy items.
Heavy items should have been distinguished within the category of "keeping in excess" (atireka);
therefore, they are not discussed separately here because they conform to the three grades treated as a single example in the subsequent text.
The one hundred and one items, such as the keeping of extra robes and so forth, constitute the lower capacity;
the Snowy Mountains constitute the superior [capacity].
This is as explained in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra: Śākyamuni, in a previous life, was once a great being (mahāsattva).
Dwelling in the Snowy Mountains, I wore only deerskin.
At that time, there were many kinds of fragrant roots, lotus roots, and *agaru* roots within the Snowy Mountains;
during that period, I remained alone therein, subsisting solely on various fruits.
Having finished eating, one should strike up mindfulness and practice seated meditation;
once the power of endurance is perfected, one will no longer frequent the human world.
In this way, one may forget such matters as the formal declaration of purity (*viśuddhi-ārocana*) and the formal undertaking of precepts (*samādāna*).
Regarding the "twelve dhūtas" and so forth:
the new translation is *dhūta*,
which means "shaking off."
The Vinaya and the Śāstras differ.
In the Vinaya, there are the practices of sitting according to the rules (yathāsana), not performing the ritual of leftover food (akṛta-avavaśeṣa), and eating only a single morsel;
however, these are not found in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra.
In the *Śāstra*, there are regulations regarding not drinking after midday and begging for food in successive order,
whereas these are absent from the *Vinaya* texts.
Furthermore, the *Vinaya* speaks of the "patchwork robe" (*nāṃgī*).
The Śāstra refers to "refuse-rags" (pāṃsukūla),
whereas the Vinaya merely mentions "begging for food.
The Śāstra further specifies that one should "constantly beg for food."
These two differ in name but agree in meaning;
the remaining ten are identical in both.
Furthermore, there are also points of disagreement between the various schools' Āgamas and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The general principle is no different.
Now, based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 68, I shall briefly set forth its characteristics.
First, regarding the *araṇya* (wilderness): there is much affliction for those living at home.
Therefore, they abandon their families and associates,
yet as teacher, disciple, and fellow student, they remain bound to one another and continue to disturb and trouble each other.
Therefore, one should dwell in an araṇya to bring about physical seclusion;
it is best to be at least three li away, and the further the better.
Once physical seclusion has been achieved, one must also achieve mental seclusion from the five desires and the five hindrances.
Second, regarding those who always beg for food, it is as explained in detail in the second Vaipulya [sūtra], and so forth.
Third, regarding those who wear rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*):
if they wander in all four directions in search of them, or if they resort to wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), [they are not true practitioners].
If, upon receiving a robe from another, one gives rise to sorrow or joy regarding its quality— whether it be good or bad—
it is as previously explained in detail concerning robes obtained within the Saṃgha, such as the case of food, and so forth;
or one may worry about thieves, robbers, and the like.
Fourth, eating at one sitting:
one reflects that even a single meal may still be an obstacle,
let alone the morning meal, the midday meal, and the afternoon meal.
Wasting half a day’s effort, one cannot practice the Way with a single-minded focus,
like those who tend to horses or pigs.
Regarding the fivefold moderation in eating:
Eating to satiety causes the belly to swell and the internal winds to become obstructed,
thereby hindering one's progress; therefore, one should leave aside one-third of the meal,
as Śāriputra did when he ate only five or six morsels.
Among the people of Qin, ten households were permitted to be satisfied with water alone;
for six months thereafter, those who did not drink even thin gruel felt their minds give rise to attachment and pleasure,
seeking various kinds of liquids and unable to maintain single-mindedness.
It is like taming a horse by placing a bridle upon it; its [wild] intent then ceases.
Those who dwell among the seven types of burial mounds find it easy to awaken to impermanence and easily attain the fruits of the Path.
Eighth, regarding those who sit beneath trees:
having accomplished the task of attaining the Way, they abandon [their former abodes] and go beneath trees—
just as the Buddha taught the Dharma, turned the wheel of the Dharma, and entered nirvana.
All were beneath trees.
As for those who sit in the open air (nava-abhyavakāśika),
some say that even sitting under a tree is like being in a half-hut, as it still gives rise to attachment.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of faults in sitting beneath a tree:
first, being drenched by rain;
second, bird droppings and venomous insects.
Regarding the ten types of constant sitting:
putting on and taking off one's robes is as pleasant as one desires;
among the four modes of deportment, sitting is foremost.
Food is easily digested and one's physical strength and energy are harmonized.
One must exert great effort for the great task of seeking the Way;
thieves are constantly watching for one's vulnerabilities, so it is not appropriate to sleep soundly.
Whether walking or standing, the mind is also easily gathered.
Eleventh, regarding begging in sequence:
one does not become attached, does not relish [the food], and does not disparage sentient beings.
With an impartial mind of compassion, one does not discriminate between the poor and the wealthy.
Regarding the twelve or thirteen robes:
laypeople often seek many, and for this reason, [monastics] may keep many.
Because the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists involve nakedness,
[the Buddha] maintains three robes— neither more nor less.
The present text, among the twelve dhūtas, refers to the "rag-robe" (pāṃśukūla) as the three robes.
Taken together, these constitute the practitioner of middle capacity.
As for the "three robes," this refers simply to the three robes themselves;
nowadays, when one possesses more than three, they are all treated as being the same as the three robes.
Some become attached to worldly affairs, while others spend the night in different realms;
this is truly because they are ignorant of the teachings and cultivate their own deluded sentiments.
Relying on these [delusions] to exalt themselves, they instead fall into ruin.
In this present text, it is judged to be "intermediate.
If it were superior, it would not reach the level of the *mṛgacarma* (deer-skin robe); if inferior, it would exceed the "one-hundred-and-one" types of extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*).
How can that which exceeds [the standard] be called the "three robes" (*tricīvara*)?
Now, it is said that the three robes differ from a single robe in being insufficient,
yet they differ from keeping extra robes and so forth in being excessive.
When going out of the village, one wears the saṃghāṭī over the other two robes.
When entering a great assembly, one wears the uttarāsaṅga over the pañcakaṇṭhaka;
when entering mountain forests, one wears only the antaravāsaka.
This is for the sake of modesty and because of the intense cold.
It is permitted to wear [robes] in layers;
these all represent a dignified deportment and are the roots of goodness for one's life.
Therefore, it is said that "one's robes and clothing are properly arranged."

Alas! The people of this world collectively grant the title of *dhūta* to those whose dress and deportment are disheveled, yet they call those whose conduct is restrained and self-controlled "adherents to signs.
Since the worldly masses do not understand this, they may be excused; rather, they are to be pitied.
The monastic community cannot distinguish between them, and they are thus objects of compassion and pity.
Those of inferior capacity abound in this land; their roots are cold and their natures are thin.
Therefore, the Great Sage universally permitted the opening of the three grades for all.
If one keeps only the one hundred and one [items],
some say that the *dharmaparyāya* (additional items) should be added.
If one keeps extra robes, they must be formally dedicated (*śuddhi*) by adding the appropriate ritual formula for their acceptance and maintenance.
Since these two categories are discussed together here, it is said that the "one hundred essentials" must be formally dedicated;
all are intended to assist the Path by alleviating the suffering of the physical body.
Beings of this kind still belong to the lowest capacity (*mṛdu-indriya*).
It is improper to claim that they are not included within the three grades of *viśuddha-puruṣa* (pure persons),
and it is utterly unacceptable to indiscriminately cite the practices of superior-grade great beings as a precedent.
However, the method of consecration (*śuddhi*) accords with the Mahāyāna;
therefore, as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
that which a bodhisattva possesses is offered as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
He then used the pure gift (śuddhaka-dāna) of a śrāvaka as an analogy,
saying: "It is, for example,
like a bhikṣu who, with his own robes and belongings, performs a pure gift by relinquishing them to his upādhyāya or ācārya."
If one realizes the single reality, this pure giving immediately becomes the dharma of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, even within the Hīnayāna, if one conforms to its practice,
it diminishes one’s own greedy sentiments and accords with the Buddha’s permissions and prohibitions.
What harm does such a principle do to a broad mind?
That one's own things belong to others is even more consistent with removing obstructions.
Moreover, receiving food and receiving medicine are matters arising from the gravity of the precepts on nature.
Carrying the alms bowl and wearing the robes are the foundations for avoiding censure;
since the nature of censure is grave, one must guard against it impartially so that one's traces do not become confused with those of the Śrāvakas, yet one remains a true Bodhisattva.
However, because their original aspiration was to escape suffering, they are judged to belong to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
How could one call it the Great Way by merely turning one's back on that [practice] while upholding this?
Furthermore, some say:
"Regarding all things whatsoever, one should maintain the perception that they are not one's own."
If it is beneficial, one should simply use it.
What is the purpose of performing the ritual of *śuddhi* (purification)?
Now, I ask.
Since these are not one's own wealth, why not employ them throughout the four seas?
Since they are beneficial, why not apply them directly to the two fields [of merit]?
Yet you confine them in deep chambers and seal them within chests and boxes.
If one harbors thoughts of another's property, one will inevitably incur transgression;
yet if one suddenly claims it as one’s own wealth, this still violates the rite of *śuddhika* (purification).
If, however, one performs the *śuddhika* rite before giving it away, what harm is there in principle?
Following one's own attachments and mental inclinations, others subsequently arise to imitate them.
Furthermore, a Great Sūtra states:
"There are four kinds of illnesses for those who have left the household life that prevent them from attaining nirvāṇa."
First is the desire for clothing;
second is the desire for food;
third is the desire for bedding and seating.
Fourth is being a cause for existence.
If one cannot practice contemplation regarding food and clothing, who could accept them?
They would not serve as causes for existence.
Regarding the "contemplation of clothing":
in the commentary (*śū*), these twelve [practices] are subsumed under the three categories of food, clothing, and dwelling;
one discusses the principles of contemplation by means of these three matters.
These are precisely the three virtues,
as explained in detail in the commentary on the account of Śāriputra (Kāśyapa).
Now, however, it is not so.
Regarding clothing, food, and dwelling, one establishes contemplative practices for each,
likewise dividing them into three grades.
As for the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* and others, those sūtras criticize the three types of cultivation, stating:
"O bhikṣus, although you have shaved your heads, you have not yet [attained] the true Dharma; the various fetters and latent tendencies still shroud you.
Although you wear the kāṣāya, your minds have not yet been dyed with the robes of the Mahāyāna Dharma."
Therefore, one knows that it is only when the mind is stained by the Mahāyāna that it truly accords with the robe of quiescence (śamatha) which it represents.
Thus, the citation from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* captures this very meaning:
"Abandoning the two—vitarka and vicāra."
The new names are vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).
The Abhidharmakośa states:
"Vitarka and vicāra are the coarseness and subtlety of the mind."
Now, observing the mind is also like this:
birth and death are coarse movements, like awakening;
the distracted mind within emptiness is subtle, like contemplation.
The mosquito is subtle and the gadfly is coarse;
this is because both extremes possess both the subtle and the coarse.
Therefore, it is said that "he deeply penetrates," and so forth.
Because it is like a mirror within the perfect [nature], it is able to illuminate everywhere;
this is called "profound penetration.
Because of this profound penetration, it possesses all characteristics.
If emptiness and the provisional were not thus, it would be like grinding pebbles.
This can be understood through the analogy provided below regarding the patience of tranquility (*śānti-kṣānti*).
By means of the Middle Way contemplation, one is adorned with the myriad virtues.
Therefore, it is not a robe cut according to worldly fashion.
It is called "not" because its underlying principle differs from worldly matters.
As for the contemplation of the three robes:
The text contains two layers of meaning.
First, it provides a general overview based on the three truths (*trisatya*),
noting that within each truth there are both craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Attachment is like heat and aversion is like cold.
Regarding the three perceptions:
the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that the three perceptions are those of desire, ill-will, and harm.
Now, let us borrow the analogy of the three types of awakening—namely, those associated with seeing, thinking, and so forth.
Thus, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, fascicle twenty, states:
"The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that these three types of awakening have various afflictions and act as enemies to the Three Vehicles."
It causes those of the three vehicles not to perceive the Buddha-nature,
and they are constantly rebuked by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Since the scriptural text states that it "causes sentient beings not to perceive the Buddha-nature," [it must be so].
Therefore, the three types of awakening can be correlated with the three delusions;
the three contemplations contemplate the three truths just as clothing covers the body.
The body is likewise threefold.
Furthermore, regarding the arising of views, one distinguishes them separately according to the three truths;
upon each truth, there are established respectively the counteractive and the object to be countered, as well as the adornment and that which is adorned.
The first [truth] is observed extensively, while the remaining two are observed concisely;
this may be understood by analogy.
Thus, it is known that upon each and every truth there are both the adornments of vision and love, as well as those of merit and wisdom.
This is because *śamatha* belongs to merit (*puṇya*) while *vipaśyanā* belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the "one hundred and one contemplations":
the extra robe assists the body, and thus it is generally understood as having the meaning of "assistance."
Therefore, on each of the three truths, auxiliary practices are required.
It is likewise for all traversed practices;
how could it be that only the primary practice remains unmoving?
The aids are likewise not other than quiescence,
as fully described in the section on the practice of the primary and auxiliary paths in conjunction.
For those of superior faculties, it refers solely to the single principle.
The meaning of the medium capacity opens up both the general and the specific;
the meaning of the inferior capacity establishes the auxiliary path.
Thus, based on a single principle, the general and specific, as well as the primary and auxiliary, together constitute a single intent.
Commentary on the Practice of Stopping and Contemplation (Zhi guan fu xing chuan hong jue), Scroll Four, Part Two.
